chapter: Changing styles, the road and nightlife
title: Ellington's Pullman car and the Armstrong band arrest
summary: Conditions eased a little with Ellington's own Pullman car; DeMichael tells of half of Armstrong's band arrested in Memphis over Johnny Collins's white wife.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did it get any better as time went on? Did you do any travelling in the '40s?

Yeah, well, I travelled -- well, things began to lighten up a little. And it got a little better, like, with Duke Ellington when he first started out. He used to -- for ears he hired a whole Pullman car, and they would pull off to the side and this was their place of sleeping and everything.
Yeah, I remember that -- Irving Mills.
Which was okay if you were at a place that had a siding.

Right, or a depot where they could pull it off, right. But they played a lot of major cities and things, and then if they were going to play in the backwoods or something like that, then they'd have to take automobile transportation or something like that, and then come back to the car.
Zolner Randolph was telling me about that infamous episode, when Louis took the big band down to New Orleans and coming back, they stopped in Memphis to get some gas or something --
And Johnny Col|in's wife was on the bus, and she was white. And they busted half the band.

Oh, yeah, right, right. That's the way conditions were. Those were crazy times. Because you were at the mercy of the law and the laws were -- maybe the Ku Klux Klan and all of that, so it was just a mixed up period in the history of this country, which now is being straightened out, and which is so -- when you look back you wonder how you made it.
